pull_request.title: storage/testing: reset injected decode failures
pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind flake

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The shared delete tests inject a transform/decode failure into the store and leave it set. `RunTestDeleteExpectedTransformOrDecodeError` never clears it on any path, and `RunTestDeleteWithConflictAndMissingExpectedTransformOrDecodeError` clears it only from inside the delete validator, so it survives whenever that validator is not reached. This adds a `defer setFailing(false)` to both, matching how the other fault-injecting helpers in `pkg/storage/testing` undo themselves (`defer revertTransformer()` in `watcher_tests.go` and elsewhere in `store_tests.go`).

That matters because nothing drains the etcd3 watch when a test tears down:

- `CacheDelegator.Stop` waits only for the consistency checker, `Cacher.Stop` only for the reflector driver.
- `watchChan.Stop` is a bare `cancel()`, and `EtcdTestServer.Terminate` is a no-op.
- `watchChan.run` does join its decode goroutines via `resultChanWG.Wait()`, but `run` is started bare and nobody waits for *it*.
- After the cancel, the `select` in `scheduleEventProcessing` can still take a buffered event and start a decode, and `decodeObj` takes no context.

So a decode can run against a still-failing store after the test that poisoned it has finished. In `pull-kubernetes-unit`, `hack/make-rules/test.sh` sets `KUBE_PANIC_WATCH_DECODE_ERROR=true`, and `TestDeleteWithConflictAndExpectedDecodeError` suppresses the resulting panic with `TestOnlySetFatalOnDecodeError(t, false)` — whose `t.Cleanup` restores the flag last. A late decode therefore panics the whole test binary.

` ` defaulting to true in 1.37 is what widened the window, by moving the decode onto a per-event goroutine.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

#141494

That issue names the wrong test. The panic happens on a background goroutine, so Go attributes it to whichever test is running at the time — the next one in file order, `TestDeleteWithSuggestionAndMissingExpectedTransformOrDecodeError`. The test that actually leaves the store failing is its predecessor, `TestDeleteWithConflictAndExpectedDecodeError`. Worth keeping the issue open until the panic stops showing up in CI.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The panic is rare — the issue reports a single occurrence, and I could not hit it in 40 runs of the two tests. Rather than guess, I forced the window with a temporary `time.Sleep(2 * time.Second)` at the top of the per-event goroutine in `scheduleEventProcessing`, then ran the two tests in file order.

Before, on master, it panics on the first iteration with the issue's stack (line numbers shifted by one by the probe):

```
--- PASS: TestDeleteWithConflictAndExpectedDecodeError (2.53s)
=== RUN   TestDeleteWithSuggestionAndMissingExpectedTransformOrDecodeError
panic: synthetic error

goroutine 341 [running]:
k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3.decodeObj(...)
	staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go:886 +0x1f5
k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3.(*watchChan).prepareObjs(...)
	staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go:832 +0xe5
k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3.(*watchChan).transform(...)
	staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go:663 +0x32
k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3.(*concurrentOrderedEventProcessing).scheduleEventProcessing.func1(...)
	staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/watcher.go:613 +0xa5
created by ...scheduleEventProcessing in goroutine 300
FAIL	k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher	4.559s
```

With this change and the same probe still in place, `-count=6` over both tests is 12/12 clean:

```
ok  	k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher	30.098s
```

The probe is not part of this PR — `watcher.go` is unchanged here. Without the fix the poisoned store is also visible as `watcher.go:665] failed to prepare current and previous objects: synthetic error` logged during the *following* test.

With the probe removed:

- `./pkg/storage/cacher/... ./pkg/storage/etcd3/... -count=1` — all packages ok
- the four fault-injection tests across both packages, `-count=10` — ok

No `_test.go` delta because the changed file is itself the shared test suite. A committed regression test would need a sleep injected into the production watch path to be deterministic, which does not seem worth carrying.

Three related things I noticed and deliberately kept out of this PR, happy to follow up on any of them:

- `cacher_test.go:206` discards its teardown (`ctx, s, _ := testSetup(...)`), leaking a cacher and an etcd server.
- `etcd3/store_test.go:220` injects a decode fault without `TestOnlySetFatalOnDecodeError`, unlike its cacher twin.
- The comment in `decodeObj` still refers to a `defer` that was removed in b3f9272d57a.

I used Claude Code while investigating the root cause and preparing this change. I have reviewed it and can explain every line.

```release-note
NONE
```

pull_request.title: fix(scheduler): handle recreated pod group update events
pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

- Fixes scheduler event handling for `PodGroup` and ` ` objects that are deleted and recreated with the same namespace and name.
- Kubernetes informers may coalesce a deletion and subsequent recreation into a single update notification.
- In this scenario, the old and new objects have the same namespace and name but different UIDs, representing different object instances.
- Previously, the scheduler's update handlers treated these notifications as ordinary updates instead of explicitly removing the old object and adding the replacement.
- Updates `updatePodGroup` and `updateCompositePodGroup` to compare the UIDs of the old and new objects.
- When the UIDs differ, the handlers process the event as a deletion of the old object followed by an addition of the new object.
- Preserves the existing update behavior when both objects have the same UID.
- Retains the resource-version equality check for same-UID objects, while ensuring a UID mismatch takes precedence over that check.
- Preserves event-handling metric semantics by recording replacement events through the delete and add handlers rather than as ordinary updates.
- Adds regression tests for both resource types, covering replacement scenarios with different UIDs.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #142930

In order to preserve the performance improvements, the fallback to cadvisor mechanism has to change. Kubelet used to fallback whenever PodSandboxStats was not implemented or returning partial data.

With container discovery disabled, cadvisor no longer tracks per-container stats, so falling back to it for partial CRI data would return empty results. Additionally, cadvisor is equally likely to return partial data for freshly created containers, making that fallback unreliable in practice.

A node may only create a   referring to a particular signer name if the pod actually mounts a podCertificate projected volume source that refers to that signer name, or if an authorization check for the user (verb=request-podcertificate-signer resource=<signerName>) succeeds.

pull_request.title: Prefer reschedulable victims when reprieving same-priority pods
pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When the preemptor fits as soon as either of two same-priority pods is
gone, the default preemption plugin picks the victim by age only, so the
later-started pod is always sacrificed. If that pod is hard-pinned to
its node (DaemonSet generated nodeAffinity, a nodeSelector matching a
single node, or an untolerated taint on every other node), its
replacement cannot start anywhere else: it cannot preempt the reprieved
same-priority pod, and its only legal node stays occupied by the
preemptor. The eviction leaves a permanently unschedulable pod, even
though evicting the other victim would have let its replacement run on
another node. See #141227 for the cluster reproduction where flipping
only the creation order flips the outcome between full recovery and a
permanently stuck DaemonSet replacement.

In the non-violating reprieve pass, this PR reprieves a same-priority
standalone victim whose replacement cannot reschedule elsewhere before
one whose replacement can, so the reschedulable victim is sacrificed
when either alone is enough for the preemptor.

The signal reads only the victim pod's own constraints: nodeSelector,
required nodeAffinity and taints. It never consults the owner, so a
Deployment pod pinned by a nodeSelector is treated exactly like a
DaemonSet pod, matching the discussion in the issue. Priority, PDB
handling and group victims keep their existing semantics:
- victims of different priority keep the priority ordering;
- only the non-violating group is reordered, so PDB violation
  classification is untouched;
- group victims (PodGroup /  ) are not classified;
- when both victims are pinned or both can reschedule, the age-based
  tie-break is preserved unchanged.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #141227

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- The reprieve ordering is only consulted when at least two
  same-priority standalone pods compete, so the common path does not
  list the node snapshot at all.
- Red/green: the repro test expects the movable victim with this change
  and fails on current master, where the pinned victim is selected.
  Controls cover both-movable, both-pinned, priority-vs-recoverability,
  a nodeAffinity pin and a three-victim case where two must be evicted.
- The constraint helper is unit tested for nodeSelector, required
  nodeAffinity, taints and the no-other-node case.
- The check calls helper.DoNotScheduleTaintsFilterFunc and
  nodeaffinity.GetRequiredNodeAffinity, the same functions the
  taint-toleration and node-affinity plugins use, so it cannot drift
  from the Filter phase. The required node affinity matcher is built
  once per pod.
- The classification is deliberately resource- and cordon-blind, as
  scoped in the issue discussion. That is safe by construction: a
  hard-pinned victim is only evicted when the reprieve pass cannot fit
  the preemptor with it present, which is exactly when its replacement
  would not fit on the node either, so evicting a pinned victim always
  strands its replacement. With uneven pod sizes, sparing the pinned
  victim can require evicting several smaller reschedulable victims
  where today one pinned victim would be evicted; their replacements
  restart elsewhere, while today's choice leaves a pod that cannot
  start anywhere.
- Full pkg/scheduler test suite is green; gofmt and go vet are clean.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
The default preemption plugin now spares a hard-pinned same-priority
victim (for example a DaemonSet pod or a pod with a nodeSelector
matching a single node) when a same-priority victim whose replacement
can run on another node is available. Previously the later-started pod
was always sacrificed, which could leave a permanently unschedulable
replacement.
```

This PR was written in part with the assistance of generative AI.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

##### Why
Latest introduction of   feature gate to CPU manager (and memory manager) checkpoints, has made future enhancements of checkpoint structure barely possible.

Depending if   is enabled or not V2 or V3 versions of checkpoints are used.
So new feature X that would like to modify checkpoint is blocked. It would require 4 versions to be possible: when both of features (X and  ) are enabled, when only one is, and when none is.

Such situation already happened:  

Because   was already merged and is part of 1.36 Kubernetes release,
this change needs to introduce new version V4 and provide smooth migration from old versions

##### What it does
This commit generalizes the CPU manager checkpoint functionality by keeping data serialized to a string, which is a pattern used in DRA checkpoints.

Instead of directly serializing the checkpoint struct, the actual checkpoint data is now stored in a separate struct which gets serialized to a string. The main checkpoint struct now contains this serialized data and a checksum of it.

This approach provides better forward/backward compatibility as the data structure can evolve without breaking existing checkpoints. It also allows for more robust error handling as deserialization issues can be caught and handled more gracefully.

The checksum is now calculated on the serialized data string rather than the struct itself, making it more reliable and consistent. File consistency is still kept as the checksum verification ensures data integrity.

Generalized checkpoint serialization is used regardless of feature gate settings. This allows future development of the checkpoint structure and enhancements for future features possible.

##### Bonus
Additionally a bug in migration of V2 to V3 was fixed.

When V3 checkpoint structure has invalid checksum and is corrupted, restoring checkpoint falls back to V2 version. However the data parts of V3 that were read remain in the structure, so the result is a hybrid of data from V3 and V2.

Use O(1) pod lookup instead of scanning all unschedulable pods when requeuing on ResourceClaim events for ResourceClaimTemplate-based claims with a pod owner reference.

#### What type of PR is this?

   /kind cleanup

   #### What this PR does / why we need it:

   Optimizes pod requeue on DRA ResourceClaim events for ResourceClaimTemplate-based claims.

   Currently, when a ResourceClaim is added or updated, the scheduler calls `MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue`, which iterates all unschedulable pods to find requeue candidates. For per-pod claims
   created from ResourceClaimTemplates, the owning pod is known from `OwnerReferences` — this PR adds `MoveOneToActiveOrBackoffQueue` which performs a direct O(1) map lookup by pod key instead of
   the O(n) scan.

   For shared claims without a single pod owner, the existing `MoveAll` path is used as fallback.

This PR introduces the `desiredCount` field to both `BasicSchedulingPolicy` and `GangSchedulingPolicy` APIs, guarded by the new `PodGroupDesiredCount` feature gate.

Currently, `minCount` defines the strict minimum number of pods required to start a workload. However, scheduling immediately upon reaching `minCount` can lead to suboptimal placement or fragmentation, as the scheduler lacks visibility into the full extent of the workload.

pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
First of four PRs splitting #143128. 

This PR changes how the Job controller finds and manages the Workload and PodGroup for a Job when   is enabled:

- Discover the Workload and PodGroup by their deterministic names through the listers. The Workload/PodGroup informer indexes are removed.
- Pick the management mode from the Job object alone, with no lookups and no special case for the owner's kind. Rules are checked in this order:
    - spec.template.spec.schedulingGroup set -> the controller manages nothing.
    - scheduling.k8s.io/workload-name or scheduling.k8s.io/group-template-name set -> the controller manages the PodGroup only.
    - spec.scheduling set -> the controller manages both the Workload and the PodGroup, whatever the owner.
    - Otherwise, a Job with a controller ownerReference gets nothing, and a Job with no owner gets both with the Basic policy.
  Jobs created by a CronJob get a Workload and PodGroup only when jobTemplate.spec.scheduling is set.
- A Job with scheduling.k8s.io/workload-name or scheduling.k8s.io/group-template-name selects the template named by group-template-name in the external Workload named by workload-name.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The `fieldSeccompProfile` function used an if-chain that silently fell through to `Unconfined` for any unrecognized `SeccompProfileType`. This means an unknown type would run the container without seccomp protection and without any error.

pull_request.body:
### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig node
/area kubelet

### What this PR does / why we need it:

With   enforced, `generateLinuxContainerResources` omits
`memory.high` from the container's Unified cgroup settings once the
container's memory request equals its limit. Runtimes merge
`UpdateContainerResources` by key and leave absent keys untouched, so an
in-place resize that raises the request up to the limit keeps the
`memory.high` throttle computed for the previous request instead of
clearing it, and nothing heals it on later syncs:

| memory request (limit 512Mi) | container memory.high |
|---|---|
| 256Mi (created) | 510025728 |
| 400Mi (resize) | 525123584 (correct) |
| 512Mi = limit (resize) | 525123584 (stale, should be max) |

This PR emits `memory.high="max"` explicitly for the `request == limit`
case, mirroring the existing  -off reset path in the same
function. Freshly created `request == limit` containers end up in the
identical kernel state either way (unset `memory.high` means
unthrottled), so creation behavior is unchanged; only the resize path
changes, from stale-throttle to correct.

pull_request.title: kubelet: resize container memory and cpu concurrently
pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/sig node

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Today, in-place container memory and CPU resizing (e.g. `kubectl patch pod <pod> --subresource resize`) happens sequentially. The kubelet makes an UpdateContainerResources gRPC call per container to set the container’s cgroup memory limit and request, one container at a time. Containers whose memory decreases are resized first, before containers whose memory increases (where a change in the limit decides the direction, and if the limit is unchanged, the request does). 

This PR changes this to a concurrent pattern, where all containers whose memory decreases are resized concurrently, and once those have finished, all containers whose memory increases run concurrently. CPU resizing follows the same pattern.

A byproduct of the concurrent cgroup resizes is that if one container's resize fails, the others in the same group are still attempted. Errors are aggregated, the remaining resize steps are skipped, and later syncs retry only the containers whose update did not succeed. This is validated in unit test.

##### Performance

The main improvement is the time the kubelet spends in doPodResizeAction for pods with many containers changing memory, measured by `kubelet_pod_resize_duration_milliseconds` (kubelet_ms column in the table below). The wall clock time a user waits, from `kubectl patch pod <pod> --subresource resize` until the pod status shows the new memory for every container, also improves (seconds column in the table below).

I measured both on a kind cluster, using a kubelet built before and after this PR. For each container count N, the script creates a pod with N containers and resizes all of them in one patch: half grow from 64Mi to 96Mi and half shrink from 96Mi to 64Mi, so both groups run. Each cell is p50 / p90 / max over 16 trials.

| N | kubelet\_ms before | kubelet\_ms after | seconds before | seconds after |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | 43 / 47.5 / 50 | 43.5 / 46.5 / 50 | 0.07 / 0.075 / 0.079 | 0.069 / 0.074 / 0.076 |
| 2 | 77.5 / 88 / 129 | 78.5 / 83 / 86 | 0.609 / 0.657 / 0.7 | 0.625 / 0.667 / 0.673 |
| 4 | 150 / 156.5 / 162 | 98.5 / 104 / 113 | 0.213 / 0.259 / 1.183 | 0.172 / 0.236 / 1.132 |
| 8 | 312 / 320.5 / 325 | 169.5 / 190.5 / 194 | 0.520 / 0.605 / 0.638 | 0.369 / 0.435 / 0.483 |
| 16 | 615.5 / 649.5 / 684 | 278 / 291 / 294 | 1.033 / 1.116 / 1.133 | 0.706 / 0.815 / 0.866 |

pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

   /kind feature
   /sig scheduling

   #### What this PR does / why we need it:

   Adds a `PreQueueingHintFn` extension point to the scheduling framework, called once per event to return a set of pod keys to evaluate instead of scanning all unschedulable pods. This addresses the O(N) requeue bottleneck identified in #138095 using the extension-point approach agreed upon in #138531.

   The DRA plugin implements `PreQueueingHintFn` for ResourceClaim events: for ResourceClaimTemplate-based claims (per-pod claims with a Pod OwnerReference), it returns only the owning pod's key, reducing the requeue path from O(N) to O(1). For shared claims or non-templated claims without a single pod owner, it returns nil to fall back to evaluating all pods
   (existing behavior).

   Additionally, ResourceClaim event handling is decoupled from the informer thread using an async workqueue, preventing the informer from blocking on scheduling queue lock acquisition during claim events.

   Both optimizations are gated behind the ` ` feature gate (alpha, default=false).

   #### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

   Fixes #138095
   Supersedes #138531

   #### Special notes for your reviewer:

   This implements the extension-point approach recommended by @pohly, @mm4tt, and @macsko in #138531 — plugin-specific logic stays in the plugin, the framework provides a generic `PreQueueingHintFn` that any plugin can implement.

   AI tools (Kiro CLI) were used to assist with development and testing of this change.


   #### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
No

pull_request.title: scheduler: only evaluate gated pods when requeuing a gated pod group
pull_request.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug
/sig scheduling

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

When a pod group (or composite pod group) is gated by a `PreEnqueue` plugin, `runPreEnqueuePlugins` stops after the first gated pod, and any pod joining an already-gated group via `addToPodGroupIfExists` is added without running `PreEnqueue` at all. Those non-gated member pods therefore have empty `UnschedulablePlugins` and `PendingPlugins`, which `isPodWorthRequeuing` treats via its "no failed plugins" fallback as `queueAfterBackoff`.

As a result, `isEntityWorthRequeuing` returned `queueAfterBackoff` for any gated group with ≥2 member pods on every cluster event registered by the gating plugin, even when the gating plugin's `QueueingHint` returned `QueueSkip` for the gated pod. Under the scheduling queue lock, the entity was deleted from `unschedulableEntities`, re-evaluated by `PreEnqueue` (where the gated pod was gated again), and re-inserted into `unschedulableEntities`—wasting `PreEnqueue` evaluations and inflating `scheduler_queue_incoming_pods_total` / `scheduler_queue_incoming_entities_total` metrics on every event. With `GangScheduling` enabled, every unscheduled pod `Add` triggers such an evaluation across all gated pod groups.

A gated entity cannot leave `unschedulableEntities` until its rejected pods pass `PreEnqueue`, so only these pod's `QueueingHint`s can determine whether an event may ungate the group. This PR updates `isEntityWorthRequeuing` to skip pods without `UnschedulablePlugins` and `PendingPlugins` when the entity is gated and has at least one gated pod. If the entity is marked gated but none of its member pods is (e.g., the gated pod was deleted from the group without re-running `PreEnqueue`), all member pods are still evaluated so the group cannot get stuck until the periodic flush.
